item.title: Spiral review: fluid responsiveness when the tests fail, non-resolving pneumonia, and lactate after valve surgery
item.itunes:title: Spiral review: fluid responsiveness when the tests fail, non-resolving pneumonia, and lactate after valve surgery
item.description:
Read along: live transcript that follows the audio

A Saturday spiral review. Fluid responsiveness and de-resuscitation with the rise and fall of starch and the CHEST trial, community-acquired pneumonia that fails to resolve, and lactate after aortic valve replacement with a worked blood gas. Journal watch on PELICAN, then a round-up of blood gas analysis, ABG interpretation, diabetes insipidus, SIADH and electrolyte replacement.

Chapters
0:00 Introduction
0:55 Revisit 1: fluid responsiveness when the tests fail
9:04 The rise and fall of the starches: CHEST
13:34 Revisit 2: non-resolving pneumonia (2025.1 Q11)
22:52 Revisit 3: lactate after valve surgery (2018.2 Q12)
30:30 Journal watch: PELICAN
33:11 Round-up: blood gas errors and alpha-stat
35:38 Round-up: the six-step gas method
38:11 Round-up: diabetes insipidus (2018.1 Q5)
42:06 Round-up: SIADH and cerebral salt wasting
44:49 Round-up: electrolyte replacement and hyperkalaemia
47:55 Before Monday

Take-home points

  1. Fluid responsiveness is a 10 to 15 percent rise in stroke volume after fluid; it is not hypovolaemia, so ask three questions: is there hypoperfusion, will fluid help, is fluid safe.
  2. Pulse pressure variation above about 12 percent is valid only when passive, in sinus rhythm, with tidal volume at least 8 mL/kg and a closed chest; otherwise use passive leg raise (cardiac output rise of 10 percent or more) or a 15-second end-expiratory occlusion (rise of 5 percent or more).
  3. CHEST (7,000 patients): starch versus saline, 90-day mortality 18.0 vs 17.0 percent, but renal replacement therapy 7.0 vs 5.8 percent (RR 1.21); SSC 2021 recommends strongly against starches.
  4. VASSPR: starting vasopressin at a noradrenaline-equivalent of 0.1 versus 0.4 mcg/kg/min did not change 28-day mortality (31.8 vs 33.0 percent).
  5. Your CAP fix: structure non-resolving pneumonia as wrong drug, complication, non-infective mimic, or different organism, and list the BAL, antigens, serology, QuantiFERON, vasculitis screen, echo, CT and biopsy.
  6. CAPE COD: hydrocortisone 200 mg/day in severe CAP without shock cut 28-day mortality from 11.9 to 6.2 percent.
  7. Your acid-base fix: Winters' expected PCO2 is 1.5 x HCO3 + 8 plus or minus 2; delta ratio 1 to 2 means pure HAGMA; correct the anion gap for albumin (add 0.25 per g/L below 40).
  8. Your DI fix: free water deficit = 0.6 x weight x (Na/140 - 1), about 8.7 L for a 70 kg man with sodium 169; correct chronic hypernatraemia by no more than 10 mmol/L per day.

Resources behind this episode

Oh's Intensive Care Manual

  • Oh's Intensive Care Manual 9e, ch 24 Haemodynamic monitoring, pp 697-745
  • Oh's Intensive Care Manual 9e, ch 58 Fluid and electrolyte therapy, pp 2326-2374
  • Oh's Intensive Care Manual 9e, ch 48 Pneumonia, pp 1968-2005
  • Oh's Intensive Care Manual 9e, ch 57 Acid-base disorders and hyperlactataemia, pp 2288-2319
  • Oh's Intensive Care Manual 9e, ch 69 Polyuria in the ICU: diabetes insipidus and other causes, pp 2726-2764

Guidelines

  • Surviving Sepsis Campaign: international guidelines for management of sepsis and septic shock 2021 (Evans et al., Intensive Care Med 2021)
  • ERS/ESICM/ESCMID/ALAT guidelines for the management of severe community-acquired pneumonia (Martin-Loeches et al., Intensive Care Med 2023)
  • Clinical practice guideline on diagnosis and treatment of hyponatraemia (Spasovski et al., Eur J Endocrinol 2014)

Landmark trials

  • CHEST: Myburgh et al. Hydroxyethyl starch or saline for fluid resuscitation in intensive care. NEJM 2012
  • 6S: Perner et al. Hydroxyethyl starch 130/0.42 versus Ringer's acetate in severe sepsis. NEJM 2012
  • CAPE COD: Dequin et al. Hydrocortisone in severe community-acquired pneumonia. NEJM 2023
  • VASSPR: Peltan et al. Effect of vasopressin initiation threshold on septic shock mortality. JAMA 2026
  • Landmark Studies in Critical Care, ch 12: Hydroxyethyl starch vs normal saline for fluid resuscitation: the CHEST trial, pp 126-132

Past College questions

  • 2025.1 Q11: Community acquired pneumonia (your mark 5.5)
  • 2013.2 Q26: Metabolic alkalosis, DKA, HAGMA, lactic acidosis (your mark 1.5)
  • 2018.1 Q5: Metabolic acidosis; hypernatraemia from diabetes insipidus (your mark 5)
  • 2016.2 Q24: Fluid responsiveness
  • 2020.2 Q17: Assessing fluid responsiveness
  • 2018.2 Q12: Causes of lactic acidosis after aortic valve replacement
  • 2012.1 Q18: Community acquired pneumonia

Journal watch

  • PELICAN: Saugel et al. Individualized cardiac index-guided hemodynamic therapy in high-risk patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery. JAMA 2026

Further reading

  • Monnet et al. Prediction of fluid responsiveness. What's new? Ann Intensive Care 2022
  • Lactate: where are we now? Crit Care Clin 2020
  • Irwin and Rippe 9e, ch 73 Life-threatening community-acquired bacterial and parasitic infections

item.title: Deep dive: rhabdomyolysis and crush, the kidney in the line of fire
item.itunes:title: Deep dive: rhabdomyolysis and crush, the kidney in the line of fire
item.description:
Read along: live transcript that follows the audio

Wednesday deep dive. Rhabdomyolysis and crush injury: where the syndrome came from, the causes the College wants by category, why the kidney fails, the calcium and phosphate traps, and what actually changes outcome. Landmark trials STARRT-AKI and PLUS, then the 2020 first-sitting rhabdomyolysis question read in full and worked by an examiner and candidate.

Chapters
0:00 Introduction
0:46 Tutorial: rhabdomyolysis and crush
15:01 Landmark trials
17:57 Exam practice

Take-home points

  1. Rhabdomyolysis is a CK more than 5 times the upper limit of normal (usually above about 1,000 U/L). Kidney injury becomes more likely above about 5,000, but CK alone predicts poorly.
  2. For 'list five causes', give five different categories with examples, at 0.5 marks each: crush or immobility, exertion or seizures, ischaemia or compartment syndrome, temperature (heat stroke, NMS, MH), drugs and toxins (statins with fibrates, propofol, cocaine), infection, and metabolic causes (low potassium or phosphate).
  3. AKI has four hits: tubular myoglobin casts in acidic urine, haem-iron oxidative injury, nitric-oxide scavenging causing vasoconstriction, and hypovolaemia from fluid sequestered in muscle.
  4. Crush fluids (ERA field guidance): isotonic saline about 1 L/h, ideally before extrication, 3 to 6 L in the first 6 hours, no potassium-containing fluid in the field. In ICU, titrate to a urine output of 1 to 3 mL/kg/h. Stop escalating if anuric and plan dialysis.
  5. Don't replace early hypocalcaemia unless there's tetany, arrhythmia or hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, because calcium deposits in muscle and rebounds as hypercalcaemia. Hypophosphataemia causes rhabdo; hyperphosphataemia is its consequence.
  6. Bicarbonate and mannitol have no RCT support (Brown 2004: no benefit with CK above 5,000). The College gives no marks either way. Dialysis is for standard indications only, not myoglobin clearance.
  7. PLUS (2022, n=5,037): balanced fluid vs saline, 90-day mortality 21.8% vs 22.0%. STARRT-AKI (2020, n=3,019): accelerated vs standard RRT, mortality 43.9% vs 43.7%, with more dialysis dependence at 90 days (10.4% vs 6.0%).
  8. Your crush question (2025.1 Q3): 4.5/10 on 12 Oct, then 7/10 on 15 Oct. When a stem says 'blood and fluid', give fluid equal weight, with a rate and a target.

Resources behind this episode

Oh's Intensive Care Manual

  • Oh's Intensive Care Manual 9e, ch 55: Acute kidney injury (pp 2245-2260), rhabdomyolysis section
  • Oh's Intensive Care Manual 9e, ch 56: Renal replacement therapy (pp 2266-2281)

Guidelines

  • Sever et al. Recommendations for the management of crush victims in mass disasters (ISN RDRTF). Nephrol Dial Transplant 2012
  • ERA crush recommendations, field version (2025)
  • KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury (2012)

Landmark trials

  • PLUS: Finfer et al. Balanced multielectrolyte solution versus saline in critically ill adults. NEJM 2022
  • STARRT-AKI: STARRT-AKI Investigators. Timing of initiation of renal-replacement therapy in acute kidney injury. NEJM 2020
  • Brown et al. Preventing renal failure in rhabdomyolysis: do bicarbonate and mannitol make a difference? J Trauma 2004

Past College questions

  • 2025.1 Q3: Crush injury and rhabdomyolysis (your marks 4.5, then 7)
  • 2020.1 Q1: Rhabdomyolysis (read in this episode)
  • 2017.1 Q5: Rhabdomyolysis
  • 2020.2 Q4: Causes of metabolic acidosis and rhabdomyolysis
  • 2025.2 Q8: Biochemistry in pancreatitis, rhabdomyolysis and Addison's disease

Further reading

  • Bywaters and Beall. Crush injuries with impairment of renal function. BMJ 1941 (the original description)
  • McMahon et al. A risk prediction score for kidney failure or mortality in rhabdomyolysis. JAMA Intern Med 2013
  • AAST Critical Care Committee. Rhabdomyolysis clinical consensus document. Trauma Surg Acute Care Open 2022
  • EAST practice management guideline: management of rhabdomyolysis. Am J Surg 2022

item.title: Shock: classify it by mechanism, prove it with the numbers
item.itunes:title: Shock: classify it by mechanism, prove it with the numbers
item.description:
Read along: live transcript that follows the audio

Consultant tutorial: defining shock, the four mechanisms with the haemodynamic pattern for each, and the limits of bedside perfusion signs in a ventilated patient. Then an examiner and candidate work a cardiogenic versus septic shock data question. Study day Wednesday 28 October.

Chapters
0:00 Tutorial: classifying shock
10:46 Exam practice: cardiogenic vs septic shock
15:32 Close

Take-home points

  1. Shock is inadequate oxygen delivery or use at the cellular level. Hypotension is common but not required (ESICM 2014 consensus).
  2. Classify by mechanism: hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, obstructive, distributive (plus cytotoxic). Mixed shock is common. In SOAP II, about 62% of shocked ICU patients were septic and about 2% obstructive.
  3. Haemodynamic patterns: hypovolaemic = low filling pressures, low output, high SVR, low SvO2. Cardiogenic = wedge high (often >18), CI <2.2 on support, high SVR, low SvO2. Obstructive = low output and high SVR, with pressures set by the site (tamponade equalises diastolic pressures within about 5 mmHg). Distributive = low SVR, normal or high output and SvO2.
  4. SVR = 80 x (MAP - CVP) / CO; normal 800-1200 dyn.s.cm-5. A high SvO2 in sepsis does not exclude tissue hypoxia.
  5. Septic shock (Sepsis-3): vasopressor needed for MAP 65 or more and lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid; hospital mortality >40%.
  6. Bedside perfusion: CRT >3 s is abnormal. ANDROMEDA-SHOCK: 28-day mortality 34.9% vs 43.4% (P = 0.06). A Pcv-aCO2 gap >6 mmHg suggests low flow. MAP 65 is the default (SEPSISPAM: no mortality difference at 80-85).
  7. Shock on day 2 after an MI: re-infarction, VSD (oxygen step-up), papillary muscle rupture (large v waves), free wall rupture with tamponade.

Resources behind this episode

Oh's Intensive Care Manual

  • Oh's Intensive Care Manual 9e, ch 23: Overview of shock (pp 671-689)

Guidelines

  • Cecconi et al. Consensus on circulatory shock and hemodynamic monitoring (ESICM task force). Intensive Care Med 2014
  • Singer et al. Sepsis-3 definitions. JAMA 2016

Landmark trials

  • SOAP II: De Backer et al. Dopamine vs norepinephrine in shock. NEJM 2010
  • ANDROMEDA-SHOCK: Hernandez et al. Peripheral perfusion vs lactate targeting. JAMA 2019
  • SEPSISPAM: Asfar et al. High vs low blood-pressure target in septic shock. NEJM 2014

Past College questions

  • 2010.1 Q16: Different causes of shock
  • 2016.1 Q18: Approach to undifferentiated shock
  • 2022.2 Q30: PA catheter data interpretation
  • 2023.1 Q1: Cardiogenic shock
  • 2024.2 Q19: Refractory vasodilatory shock

Further reading

  • Vincent and De Backer. Circulatory shock (review). NEJM 2013

item.itunes:summary:
Consultant tutorial: defining shock, the four mechanisms with the haemodynamic pattern for each, and the limits of bedside perfusion signs in a ventilated patient. Then an examiner and candidate work a cardiogenic versus septic shock data question. Study day Wednesday 28 October.
Take-home points: 1. Shock is inadequate oxygen delivery or use at the cellular level. Hypotension is common but not required (ESICM 2014 consensus). 2. Classify by mechanism: hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, obstructive, distributive (plus cytotoxic). Mixed shock is common. In SOAP II, about 62% of shocked ICU patients were septic and about 2% obstructive. 3. Haemodynamic patterns: hypovolaemic = low filling pressures, low output, high SVR, low SvO2. Cardiogenic = wedge high (often >18), CI <2.2 on support, high SVR, low SvO2. Obstructive = low output and high SVR, with pressures set by the site (tamponade equalises diastolic pressures within about 5 mmHg). Distributive = low SVR, normal or high output and SvO2. 4. SVR = 80 x (MAP - CVP) / CO; normal 800-1200 dyn.s.cm-5. A high SvO2 in sepsis does not exclude tissue hypoxia. 5. Septic shock (Sepsis-3): vasopressor needed for MAP 65 or more and lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid; hospital mortality >40%. 6. Bedside perfusion: CRT >3 s is abnormal. ANDROMEDA-SHOCK: 28-day mortality 34.9% vs 43.4% (P = 0.06). A Pcv-aCO2 gap >6 mmHg suggests low flow. MAP 65 is the default (SEPSISPAM: no mortality difference at 80-85). 7. Shock on day 2 after an MI: re-infarction, VSD (oxygen step-up), papillary muscle rupture (large v waves), free wall rupture with tamponade.
